That isn't social Darwinism; it's actual Darwinism. And to be even more pedantic, I'd say that the answer depends on your definition of "failure." Darwinism is about species, not individuals; there are no value judgements about an individual organism's survival. Arguably the only "failure" in Darwinism is extinction, and the survival of a "successful" species necessarily depends on the survival of some individual organisms and the death of others. In other words, if you have "good genes" and fail to pass them on, then the species may come ever so slightly closer to extinction. However, if you have "bad genes" and fail to pass them on, then the species could become slightly less likely to go extinct. So I don't think a Darwinist would call a man a failure just for not having progeny.

I don't think human beings have any practical reproductive imperative or necessary participation in biological evolution given that our culture now deals primarily in an epigenetic or cultural human legacy. It is a mistake, I think, to presume some purpose to evolution and the individual's participation in it. Natural evolution is not a process of optimization with any sort of long-term objective that there's any responsibility to. Instinctual biological drives really have no relevance when we now have many different artificial ways of reproducing--with many more on the way. For human beings, DNA is becoming an STL file. Many argue that it's irresponsible to reproduce at all given the problem of overpopulation, though that's largely a problem of standard-of-living effects. Birthrates have long been in decline with the aging of the population in the developed world--moving toward situations like we see in Japan--because low child mortality, high cost of child-rearing, availability of contraception, an ability to save income long-term, and institutional old-age support have replaced the need for children as a safety net in old age. The more control we have over biology and our economic destiny, the less inclined we are to reproduce because, fundamentally, it's a hassle. In the developing world, birthrates are high as a hedge against high child mortality given poor health care systems and a need for larger families to meet their aged members' support. Old fashioned Malthusianist convention, rooted in racism and classism, has long suggested the poor needed poverty to suppress their numbers because of an inherent, animalistic, tendency to reproduce. But the fact of the matter is a simple and rational economic proposition. Widespread application of Universal Basic Income could actually stop overpopulation.

So there's really nothing that important about passing along a genetic heritage--especially since it's about to all be up for editing at will anyway and, eventually, a lot of 'children' won't even be organic. All that really matters is the love.
